client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago, kind of out of nowhere, and it's been really hard to be around my friends lately because they all seem to have just... moved on with their lives. Like they'll invite me out and everyone's laughing and talking about normal stuff, and I just feel this huge distance between me and them, like I'm on the other side of a glass wall. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep feeling this isolated.
therapist: What you're describing — that feeling of being behind glass while life carries on around you — is such a painful and isolating experience, and it makes complete sense that grief can create that kind of distance, especially when it feels like the world didn't pause the way you needed it to. I also notice that even in sharing something so heavy, there's a kind of quiet exhaustion in how you're carrying this, like you've been holding it for a long time without a real place to put it down. I'm really glad you decided to try something, and I want you to know this is a space where we don't have to rush past any of it — what feels most important to start with today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess what feels most important is just... why I still feel so stuck, even though it's been almost two years since my dad died. Everyone around me has kind of moved on, or at least they act like they have, and I feel like there's something wrong with me for not being able to do the same. It's exhausting pretending I'm okay when I'm really just going through the motions every single day.
therapist: There's nothing wrong with you for still feeling this — grief doesn't follow a timeline, and the exhaustion of performing "okay" every day is its own kind of weight on top of the loss itself. I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds almost... braced, like you're holding yourself very carefully, maybe trying to get through saying it without fully letting it land. I'm curious — when you're alone, away from the pretending, what does the grief actually feel like then?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: When I'm alone... it's like this heavy, suffocating quiet that just sits on my chest. I'll be doing something completely normal, like making tea or whatever, and then it just hits me that she's gone and I kind of freeze up and don't know what to do with myself. I don't cry as much as I think I'm supposed to, which honestly makes me feel worse, like maybe I didn't love her enough or something.
therapist: That thought — "maybe I didn't love her enough" — is such a painful place for your mind to go, and I want to gently challenge it: the absence of tears doesn't measure the size of love, it often just means the grief is so big the body doesn't quite know how to hold it. I also notice that as you're describing something so raw and overwhelming, your voice has gone very soft and quiet, almost like part of you is stepping back from the full weight of what you're saying. I wonder — is it possible that the "freezing up" you describe, and even the quietness right now, might be your mind's way of protecting you from something that still feels too large to fully face?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think you might be right that I'm holding back, but I'm not sure if it's protection or just... numbness, honestly. Like, I can't tell anymore whether I'm being careful with myself or whether I've just gone somewhere flat and empty inside. And part of me worries that if I actually let myself feel the full weight of it, I won't be able to come back from that.
therapist: That fear — "what if I fall into it and can't come back" — is one of the most common things that keeps grief frozen in place, and it makes so much sense that you'd build walls around something that feels that vast. What I want to offer you is that in my experience, people who worry about not coming back are usually the ones who do — it's often the ones who feel *nothing* who are in more danger of staying lost. Can we sit with this a little: when you imagine actually letting yourself feel it, what do you picture happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I picture just... completely falling apart. Like, ugly crying on the floor and not being able to stop, and then having to go back to work or pick up groceries or whatever, and everyone just knowing that something is broken in me. I guess what scares me most is that if I really let it out, there won't be anything left underneath — like the grief is the only thing holding the shape of who I was with him.
therapist: What you just said is so profound and important — "the grief is the only thing holding the shape of who I was with her" — because it points to something that isn't brokenness at all, but love that doesn't have anywhere to go yet. The fear isn't really about falling apart; it's about losing the last living connection to who you were when she was here. I want to gently offer that grief doesn't hollow you out when you face it — it slowly makes room for you to carry her differently, not less, just in a way that doesn't have to hurt quite this much all the time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but I'm scared that if the grief changes shape, if it hurts less, it means I'm somehow moving on from her, like I'm choosing to forget. It feels like betrayal, even though I know logically that's probably not what you mean. How do you carry someone differently without it feeling like you're just... leaving them behind?
therapist: The fear that healing equals forgetting is one of the most tender and universal parts of grief, and I want you to know that feeling it doesn't mean your logic is wrong — it means you loved her deeply enough that even the idea of relief feels like a risk. Carrying someone differently isn't leaving them behind; it's more like moving them from a wound you keep pressing on to a place inside you that's actually built to hold them — where they become part of how you see the world, the things you notice, the person you're still becoming. Can I ask — are there small moments, even now, where you catch yourself thinking "she would have loved this" or "I got that from her"? Because those moments are already you carrying her forward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, those moments do happen. Like last week I was at the farmers market and I saw these ridiculous sunflowers, the big messy kind, and I just immediately thought "Mom would have bought every single one of those." But then it hurt so much that I almost wished I hadn't noticed them at all, you know? Like those moments don't feel like carrying her forward, they feel like getting ambushed.
therapist: That image — you, standing in front of those big messy sunflowers, feeling her so completely — is actually one of the most beautiful and painful things you've shared, and "ambushed" is exactly the right word for how grief works when love is still that alive. I notice you're speaking about it very softly, almost tenderly, like even the memory of that moment is something fragile you're holding carefully. What if those ambushes aren't grief attacking you, but her finding you — and the pain is just how love feels when it has nowhere to land yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe... I want to hold onto it, I really do, but part of me wonders if it's just a prettier way of saying the same painful thing. Like, does it actually change anything if I think of it as her finding me instead of grief ambushing me? I'm still standing in a grocery store parking lot barely holding it together.
therapist: That's a really honest and important pushback, and you're right to name it — a reframe isn't a painkiller, and it doesn't stop you from standing in that parking lot with shaking hands. But here's what it can do over time: it's the difference between your nervous system reading those moments as *attacks* to brace against, versus something you slowly learn to breathe through, even when it's hard. Can we think together about what you actually needed in that moment at the farmers market — not a reframe, but practically, what would have helped you feel less alone with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... what would have helped is if someone had just noticed. Like if my friend had looked over and seen that I was struggling instead of just chatting away about the tomatoes or whatever. It sounds so small when I say it out loud, but I think I just needed someone to check in on me without me having to ask for it, because asking feels impossible in those moments.
therapist: That doesn't sound small at all — it sounds like one of the most human needs there is, to be *seen* in a hard moment without having to perform the vulnerability of asking for it. I notice as you said that, your voice got very quiet and quick, like maybe even naming that need feels a little exposing, as if wanting to be noticed is somehow asking too much. I want to reflect back to you that what you're describing — needing someone to reach toward you — isn't a burden you're placing on others; it's actually something you deserve, and I wonder if part of our work together might be exploring why asking for that feels so impossible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, you're right that I got quiet, and I kind of hate that you noticed that, honestly. It's like even being seen in this room, right now, makes me want to take it back and say "no, I'm fine, forget I said anything." I think part of me genuinely believes that needing people to reach out to me is selfish, like I'm expecting them to do work I should just do myself.
therapist: The fact that you "kind of hate" being seen right now, even as you're describing exactly how much you need it — that tension is so important, and it takes real courage to stay in the room with it rather than retreating into "I'm fine." That belief that needing others is selfish didn't come from nowhere — I'm curious, is that a message you learned somewhere along the way, maybe even from watching how the people around you handled their own needs?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
